Almost like GTA V except I like it more. Phantom Liberty is the mandatory add-on, don't skip this.
And no bugs, running smoothly.

My playthrough:
1. Main story until open city
2. Did all possible side jobs, gigs and NCPD tasks 
3. Continued main story and finished "Playing for Time" until "Tapeworm"
4. Completed other side jobs now available
5. Started "Dog Eat Dog" - start and finish Phantom Liberty
6. Continue main story final chapters aka Act3, starting with "Nocturne Op55N1"

Some tips:
+ You can do Cyberpsycho tasks, gigs and other side jobs to learn the city and level up before continuing the main story.
+ I prefer driving with bike for faster access between traffic jams.
+ Avoid walkers, I don't wish to deal with cops if I accidentally hit hard some walkers.
+ Sometimes the sniper rifle and distance are Your best friends.
+ Listening the radio is important part of the game, it's easy to add custom radio stations with mods. I added Legendary FM and Raadio Elmar.

review:
It's an ok game with an interesting story and mostly good combat, but dear god is it bug ridden which is incredibly disappointing for a 5+ year old game coming from CDPR. It has:
- Floating items/NPCs in so many different spots/situations.
- NPCs that are constantly getting stuck, including during quest lines and require reloading from the last checkpoint.
- Random crashes.
- Some visual glitches.

Other issues include:
- Terrible melee combat
- Lots of scripted events with some not making sense
- Lots of repeated dialog

What's good:
- Visuals. Probably the coolest looking city in any game I've played.
- Gunplay is good.
- Lots of variety in quests
- Lots of customization
- A pretty good story

I played about 2-3 years ago and refunded because the city didn't feel real or alive and the gameplay just felt stale/off. I tried playing again via the family sharing and was hooked after 5 hours and bought the main game and DLC. I'm into Act 3 and was going to through the Phantom Liberty DLC area but after having another stuck NPC that required reloading from the last checkpoint and being in the middle of a boss fight and having another random crash I think I'm done. It's too immersion breaking and I think CDPR tried doing too much without smoothing out the large number of issues I'm seeing this game.

It sucks because I think this could be a really great game, but fails due to what I think was adding content without fixing existing issues. If I see I major bug patches (unlikely at this point) I might come back.

Edit: So a couple days went by and I found myself wanting to keep pushing through. I started taking a little more time and overall I do think it's a decent game with fun moments. I just really wish they would've polished it out more and made it feel more real.

review:
overall I love the game and the DLC. 
Story is great with lots of interesting characters. Map design and setting have LOADS of detail making it all very immersive and feel real. TONS of interesting in-game lore for you to dive into if you're really invested into the game. 
Fighting enemies can be a drag because of how bullet spongy enemies and the player can be, especially in the early game. This lessens as your character gets stronger but it kind of depends on how you build your character. I went with stealth, netrunner, power sniper, and pistol so I was doing a lot of one and two shotting. 
Character progression is solid however when it comes to getting better weapons you at times are just getting a slightly better clone of your original gun, katana, bat, knife, etc. Gun play can feel wonky at first you kind of got to get used to it. 
Despite all the updates the game can be buggy at times but there are mods that fix this.
Driving controls feel terrible and the stated speed of your vehicle feels fake. 200 MPH feels like 80-110 in GTA5. If you drive too fast ♥♥♥♥ won't even render in fast enough.
Optimization is pretty horrible, one of the most demanding games on a system on the market. I have RTX 4060 and 16GBs of RAM and I'm getting an average of like 30 FPS at 2k resolution.

review:
This is, hands down, one of the best things I've ever played. It's got a huge, complex setting that's brilliantly and beautifully realized. It's got a story that stays engaging from start to finish. It's got characters so deep and well written that you actually end up caring about them.

The player-character builds are astonishing. On my second playthrough I played a sort of cyber-ninja, all souped up to the point I could clear a room with just a katana and some throwing knives before anybody knew what was happening. It was genuinely an incredible experience. But here's one word of warning: don't try to be a jack-of-all-trades. This character system hugely rewards specialization, and specialized characters are so much fun that it's worth playing again and again just to have those different experiences across different specializations. That, and each playthrough is like a blast of nostalgia, and you get to see all those people and places you've missed. It ain't real life, but it'll do in a pinch.

I rate this as one of the true masterpieces of gaming. Don't miss it.

review:
After putting in the time to 100% complete Night City, I can confidently say Cyberpunk 2077 is an absolute blast and worth every single penny. The world, the characters, the music, and the raw atmosphere are a straight 10/10. Night City is easily one of the most detailed and gorgeous open worlds ever made, and running it with DLSS and Frame Generation is pure eye candy it runs beautifully, even with a few minor bugs lingering around.
The movement feels super fluid and the side gigs are fantastic, but the gunplay never fully clicked for me. It feels more serviceable than exceptional. Only a handful of hand cannons, snipers, and shotguns actually feel satisfying to shoot, while most ARs and SMGs just feel underwhelming. Plus, even on Hard, the game rarely gave me a real challenge looking back, I definitely should’ve bumped it up to Very Hard.
My main gripes come down to some uneven pacing, a few noticeable plot holes, and a surprisingly short list of true, memorable boss fights. You just can’t shake the feeling that a lot of content was left on the cutting room floor. But honestly, those flaws only stick out because the rest of the game is so damn good. They just make you realize how heartbreakingly close this came to being a completely flawless masterpiece. Throw in the Phantom Liberty DLC, which is absolute cinema from start to finish, and you’re looking at one of the best RPGs ever made. It’s not perfect, but it’s still a masterpiece in its own right, and an experience I won’t forget anytime soon.

review:
Cyberpunk 2077 had a rocky release due to the premature release, but it eventually redeemed itself with the release of Phantom Liberty along with several quality of life improvements. Now, it would be safe to say that Cyberpunk 2077 is in a playable state, although not perfect by any means. It is still possible run into some bugs, and the AI still needs adjustments, especially for the pedestrians. They simply jump in front of the car, causing NCPD to tail you unnecessarily.

However, they’re not too big of a problem to take you out of the experience. Night City looks astonishing, the combat feels great, and the story pulls you in just fine. Can’t forget about the amazing soundtrack as well. All in-game soundtrack and the radio stations are simply bangers that they got me hooked the day I started playing it.

As I’ve mentioned before, the game used to be a wreck, therefore; I purposely waited for them to sort out the kinks before playing, and I don’t regret that decision. It was marketed as an open world RPG initially and I believe it still qualifies as one despite many claim it isn’t. There’s an in-depth character customization, and many skill trees to choose from as well as implants that can personalize your experience according to your tastes and needs.

Depending on which skill tree you chose to upgrade, the gameplay changes drastically. They can even be combined with others to create a hybrid build. Furthermore, Phantom Liberty adds the additional Relic Tree to flesh out the already existing builds. There are simply too many possibilities that it would be unfair to say that there isn’t enough to lead a unique experience.

The story is where the game shines best, as many have already stated before. However, the main missions are mostly focused on world-building, thus they lack enough combat to make you properly appreciate what the game truly offers. Nevertheless, Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t a game that should be breezed through. One should tackle side quests too if they want to unlock the other endings and see the bond between V and other characters.

Johnny Silverhand’s story also gets fleshed out and told mostly through side quests. Many also claim that Keanu Reeves’ involvement ruined what could’ve been a great game otherwise, but I’m inclined to disagree with that take. While it is true that his involvement happened quite late in development and led to many rewrites in the script, I’d say it turned out great.

The only aspect that left me a bit disappointed was the fact that V’s background doesn’t impact that story as much as I had hoped. The only truly different part, depending on your background, is the introduction mission and how you ended up in Night City and met Jackie Welles. All in all, Cyberpunk 2077 is a must-play. You could also watch Edgerunners to get a better grasp on the universe it is based on.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Despite having a rocky headstart, Cyberpunk 2077 managed to pull itself together with Phantom Liberty as well as other patches. It offers a great storyline, strong combat, and a heavily customizable experience. The soundtrack is also noteworthy, and the universe it was built upon feels real in all aspects!

review:
Elden Ring was my first FromSoft game. I play very few 3rd-person action games, and very few open-world RPGs, so I was way out of my element. However, by the end of my 225-hour playthrough, I loved it! Elden Ring was an epic adventure unlike any other I have played.

I played without using the wiki or any external guide other than seeking occasional hints from a trusted friend.

My favorite aspect of Elden Ring was the world and level design. The towering verticality, the epic scale of it, the huge vistas. I loved how the world was designed to showcase views of faraway castles and mountaintops, enticing me to discover and explore them. I loved the way the dungeons and sub-areas twist and wind on themselves, making clever use of vertical space. Exploration is one of my favorite activities in video games, and Elden Ring was a dark wonderland of discovery. There were constant surprises waiting in every tunnel, behind every castle wall, atop every rugged peak.

The 3rd-person melee combat was very unfamiliar to me. It was brutally difficult initially, but I used loading screens tips to gradually learn some mechanics. I lacked the dexterity and experience to properly time melee attacks, dodge-rolls, and blocks, so I brute-forced my way through much of the game by attacking with ranged spells and running away.

Even if I never got very good at the combat, I was glad that levelling up my character had a meaningful impact on my success. Whenever I was not able to progress in a certain area because the enemies were too hard, I could always go somewhere else to make progress, then come back later with better stats and gear. This was a huge upside to the open-world design.

Ultimately, the game felt tough but (mostly) fair. It did provide many conveniences to the player -- for example, never losing my loot, and using the same currency for levelling up as for purchasing at merchants. The generous abundance of instant-travel points and the tireless double-jumping super-horse made map traversal easy.

My least favorite aspect of Elden Ring was the unwieldy feeling of having to manage character animations constantly. Getting smacked by an enemy while my character slowly did his "stand up" animation. Some animations queued; some didn't. Some animations could be cancelled, some couldn’t. Not being able to block because I'm still doing a spell cast animation. Going off a cliff because my horse had to do its "turning around" animation. And most fatal of all, the unstoppable "I'm out of mana potions" animation.

Elden Ring features a quest system which is very obscured to the player (i.e. no quest log, no quest markers) but is also very conditional (i.e. there are unseen conditions determining whether a quest can even be started, progressed, or completed). Unfortunately, this is a very player-unfriendly combination. I appreciate games which don't hold the player's hand, and as such I kept a very large and thorough document about leads and mysteries I wanted to pursue. However, I found instances where a quest character did not appear where they were supposed to, because I hadn't reached some other unrelated checkpoint yet. Or reaching some unrelated checkpoint caused the quest character to not appear, despite the insistence to the contrary of some clue or dialogue I had found. There were also instances where reaching a destination was not tied to any intuitive geographical progression or clues, but by finding a teleport from one arbitrary location to another.

Anyway, those gripes aside, Elden Ring was an incredible journey, full of struggles and triumphs. Exploring and discovering this dark and mysterious world was fully absorbing, and I felt incredibly accomplished when I finally reached the end.

review:
[h1] One of the greatest and highest-quality games ever made. [/h1]

I’ve been putting this game off for a long time because, honestly, I’m not a big fan of open-world games. Too many of them feel bloated, repetitive, and filled with busywork and i get lost and frustrate easily. Elden Ring is different. This is open-world done right. The map is massive, but it never feels like lazy copy-paste filler. Every region feels distinct: different enemies, different bosses, different environments, and different challenges. Exploration is constantly rewarded—whether it’s a powerful weapon, a new spell, a hidden dungeon, or lore that makes you stop and think. You’re not just wandering for the sake of it; the game respects your time and curiosity.

Elden Ring doesn’t rely on cutting-edge, photorealistic graphics—and it doesn’t need to. The art direction is absolutely stunning. There were multiple moments where I literally put the controller down just to stare at the scenery. This game is living proof that art direction > realism every single time.

The character and boss designs are incredible. Every major boss feels unique, intimidating, and straight-up badass. Add in the phenomenal soundtrack, and every boss fight feels like an epic event. Even when you’re getting absolutely destroyed, you can’t help but appreciate how cool everything looks and sounds.

The combat is easily the best part of the game. The combat is deep, satisfying, and insanely flexible. There are countless ways to play: different classes, builds, weapons, spells, and playstyles. This gives the game ridiculous replay value—you could finish it multiple times and still feel like you’re playing something new.

Boss fights are intense and memorable, but also frustrating as hell—sometimes in the funniest way. Some bosses will start an attack, stall for what feels like 20 years (just like my government), and then drop it on you the moment you least expect it. Painful? Yes. Memorable? Absolutely.

I’m not going to sugarcoat it: this game is hard. That said, it’s more forgiving than other Souls games thanks to mechanics like spirit summons and co-op options. The difficulty feels challenging rather than unfair, and the game gives you tools to overcome obstacles—if you’re willing to experiment and adapt.

The story is dark, mysterious, and incredibly alluring—but it won’t hold your hand. There are no 20-minute cinematics explaining everything, no quest logs telling you exactly where to go. If you don’t pay attention to NPC dialogue, item descriptions, and environmental clues, you will get lost.

The narrative is told in fragments, pieced together by the player. It’s written by Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R. R. Martin, so expect heavy themes of decay, tragedy, and a world on the brink of collapse. If you want a straightforward, cinematic story, this isn’t it—but if you enjoy deep lore and worldbuilding, it’s one of the best in modern gaming.

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]

If you have the patience of a saint and the curiosity of a cat, buy this game. If you value your blood pressure, maybe think twice. But skipping Elden Ring means missing out on one of the most ambitious, rewarding, and unforgettable gaming experiences ever made.

review:
Elden Ring is one of the most impressive open-world RPGs ever made. Developed by FromSoftware and directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game combines the challenging combat the studio is known for with a massive world full of exploration, secrets, and unforgettable encounters.

The Lands Between is a stunning setting that constantly rewards curiosity. Every region feels unique, from haunting castles to underground cities hidden beneath the world. Unlike many open-world games, exploration rarely feels repetitive because there is always something interesting around the next corner.

Combat is deep and satisfying, offering a huge variety of weapons, spells, and character builds. Boss battles are a major highlight, requiring skill, patience, and strategy. While the difficulty can be intimidating for newcomers, the game's open structure allows players to explore elsewhere and grow stronger before tackling tougher challenges.

The story is mysterious and often told through environmental details, item descriptions, and character interactions. This approach won't appeal to everyone, but it creates a sense of discovery that fits the game's world perfectly.

The few drawbacks include occasional performance issues and a lack of traditional quest tracking, which can sometimes leave players confused about where to go next. However, these flaws are minor compared to the overall experience.

Overall, Elden Ring is a masterpiece that successfully blends challenging gameplay, rewarding exploration, and rich world-building. Whether you're a longtime fan of FromSoftware games or a newcomer looking for an unforgettable adventure, it is a game well worth playing.

review:
The first five minutes of this game went something like this:

*"I'm finally going to attend Hogwarts!"*

Twenty hours later...

*"Professor, I know you wanted me in Herbology, but I was a little busy breaking into goblin camps, adopting magical beasts, solving Merlin's 847th puzzle, and accidentally becoming the most feared wizard in Scotland."*

Hogwarts Legacy absolutely nails the fantasy of receiving your Hogwarts letter... even if it quickly forgets you're supposed to be a student.

Walking through the castle never gets old. Every hallway has something weird happening, portraits are roasting each other, staircases refuse to cooperate, and you'll spend an embarrassing amount of time opening doors just because you heard a suspicious little "ding." The amount of detail packed into Hogwarts is honestly ridiculous. You can tell this place was built by people who genuinely love the Wizarding World.

Combat completely caught me off guard. I expected a simple "wave wand, cast spell" system.

Instead, I found myself juggling enemies like I was auditioning for Wizard Kombat.

Levioso.
Accio.
Incendio.
Expelliarmus.
Repeat until everyone involved questions their life choices.

Then there's the Room of Requirement, which somehow transformed me from a student into an interior designer with a side hustle in magical wildlife conservation. I came here to learn spells. I left with a thriving beast sanctuary and enough decorative furniture to open an IKEA for wizards.

Could the game have had more meaningful choices? Definitely.

Would I have liked deeper companion relationships? Absolutely.

Did I still spend an unhealthy amount of time flying around on a broom because it made me feel like an eleven-year-old again?

Without question.

This game isn't trying to reinvent open-world RPGs. It's trying to answer one question:

*"What's it like to finally live in the Wizarding World?"*

And honestly... it absolutely delivers.

Now if you'll excuse me, I have an urgent appointment to ignore my homework, pet a Mooncalf, and commit what can only be described as an alarming number of magical felonies against poachers.

10 points to whichever house lets me skip class.

review:
**Pros:**

Beautiful open world, great graphics, and a genuinely magical atmosphere. The soundtrack is lovely, and Hogwarts Castle is absolutely enormous. Honestly, I can see where those years of development went—the castle alone is incredibly detailed and a joy to explore. The world feels immersive and believable, and simply wandering around is fun.

One thing I really appreciate is that the game doesn't rely on characters from Harry Potter's era. It stands on its own while taking place in the Wizarding World, with small references to familiar names like the Weasley and Black families. The game is definitely banking on nostalgia—let's not pretend otherwise—but I respect that it tries to carve out its own identity instead of endlessly recycling Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Voldemort.

The main story is easy to get through, and locations like Hogsmeade are charming and cozy. Combat is surprisingly fun, too. Instead of just spamming basic attacks, you can get creative by combining force, levitation, and environmental spells to approach fights in different ways.

The ambience and soundtrack are incredibly comforting. If the game had something like the Discovery Tour mode from Assassin's Creed Origins, I would have spent even more time in it.

For context, I played over 200 hours, completed every side quest, collected everything, suffered through every Merlin Trial, and grinded out all the Steam achievements. If you grew up loving Harry Potter and still enjoy the Wizarding World, this is absolutely a comfort game. It's very accessible and relaxing—although I personally hate calling games "cozy."

That said, aside from Sebastian and Ominis, none of the companions or side characters left much of an impression on me. I also think the game would have been significantly better if the developers had been willing to lean into actual RPG mechanics like consequences, reputation systems, curfews, and meaningful choices. Instead, it feels like they played it safe and made the most broadly appealing Harry Potter game possible without taking many risks.

**Cons:**

The game was announced in 2018, which in hindsight feels way too early considering it didn't release until 2023.

Most importantly: this is not an RPG, despite being marketed as one. None of your choices matter. No matter what decisions you make, the story reaches essentially the same conclusion.

**Spoilers:** Even if you choose to absorb all the ancient magic and embrace the so-called "dark path," nothing meaningful changes. The game constantly presents choices but never commits to their consequences.

The lack of consequences is a problem throughout the entire game. Why am I a 17-year-old student casually killing goblins and poachers in the forest? Why am I sneaking out every night, using forbidden magic, and fighting alongside classmates without anyone caring? At a certain point, I started wondering how my character was morally better than the people we were supposedly fighting against. The game insists the goblins are the villains, yet my character probably racks up a much higher body count than they do.

Another huge missed opportunity is Hogwarts itself. The developers spent years creating one of the most detailed versions of the castle ever seen in a game, then gave us surprisingly little to do inside it. There are classes, but they're mostly cutscenes. There's no class schedule, no attendance system, no house points, no curfew, and barely any interaction with student life. The castle looks amazing, but often feels strangely lifeless.

Sure, I can pet every cat I come across, but I can't sit in a chair. I can't lie down in my dormitory bed. I can't even sleep to pass the time of day. Somehow, Hello Kitty Island Adventure offers more role-playing immersion in those areas.

Please stop being afraid of making a real RPG. You have one of the biggest fantasy franchises in the world and a massive budget. Take some risks. Give us consequences. Give us systems. Let us actually live as Hogwarts students instead of just touring a beautiful museum.

review:
[b]Hogwarts Legacy — A beautiful spell with shallow depth[/b]

Hogwarts Legacy undeniably succeeds at one crucial thing: it makes you feel the magic. From the very first hours, the game captures the atmosphere of Hogwarts and the wizarding world with real care. The castle itself, its surroundings, and the visual effects are crafted beautifully — wandering through the halls, flying over the landscapes, and exploring iconic locations genuinely evokes that long-lost feeling of being part of a magical school.

The environments are the game’s strongest asset. Hogwarts looks stunning, the art direction is strong, and the spell effects are visually satisfying. At times, the game almost carries itself purely on atmosphere — and for a while, that’s enough.

However, once the initial sense of wonder fades, the cracks become obvious. The story is… serviceable at best. From early on, it’s clear where everything is going, and there’s little to no intrigue or narrative tension. The plot rarely surprises, and the lore is barely explained or expanded upon, which feels like a missed opportunity in such a rich universe.

Mechanically, the game can be frustrating. The constant transition moments between locations — standing in front of doors waiting for areas to load — break immersion. Even more irritating are the invisible walls inside Hogwarts itself, where you should logically be able to jump or move freely, but simply can’t. In a game built around exploration and freedom, these limitations feel especially noticeable.

In the end, Hogwarts Legacy is an emotionally effective but shallow experience. It nails the fantasy of being there, but doesn’t back it up with a compelling story or refined world interaction.

Worth playing once for the atmosphere and visuals — but once the magic wears off, there’s little reason to return.

6/10 — A beautiful visit to Hogwarts, but not a journey you’ll want to repeat.

review:
Score 7,2 out of 10

Game Visuals and Artwork : 10
Game Sound and Music : 8
Core Loop And Gameplay : 8
Character Design and story : 7
Technical Aspect/Friendly user interface : 5
Longevity And Replayability : 6
Fun and Overall Feeling : 7

Game Visuals and Artwork: 10
Hogwarts Legacy is visually stunning, clearly crafted by passionate fans of the franchise. The world is immersive and brimming with life, with incredible attention to detail that invites you to explore for hours. The combat animations are exceptionally well done, bringing the game to life in ways I never imagined possible.

Game Sound and Music : 8
The voice acting is solid, and the soundtrack hits the right notes, though it could have reached more epic heights in certain moments. Menu sounds are a thoughtful touch, and the ambient chatter from NPCs and animals as you explore adds a rich, immersive layer to the world.

Core Loop And Gameplay : 8
Hogwarts Legacy tries to strikes a balance between exploration and student life. One moment you're battling dark wizards, the next you're solving puzzles or attending classes to learn new spells. As an openworld game, it encourages you to take on a wide range of tasks, many of which reward you with gear upgrades, increased inventory space, or new cosmetic options. The variety is good, spanning from light puzzles to intense combat, though some tasks can start to feel repetitive, especially when required for progression. Combat is engaging for a while thanks to a clever shield system that forces you to use different spells to break enemy defenses, keeping encounters dynamic and satisfying. 

Character Design and story: 7
You can create your own wizard or witch with a decent range of customization options, choose your Hogwarts house, and freely transmog your character’s appearance throughout the game. While the main storyline is largely predetermined, there are a few choices to make along the way. The game is rich in dialogue and lore for those who seek it, but many of the quests feel flat and uninspired, making it difficult to stay emotionally invested. The main narrative starts off engaging, but I found myself struggling to stay interested by the end. 

Technical Aspect/Friendly user interface: 5
To get the game running above 10 FPS, I had to rely on multiple YouTube tutorials, which is unacceptable for a modern release. While I haven’t experienced hard crashes, there was significant stuttering during specific actions. After fine tuning the settings, performance has been stable. The graphics settings offer a lot of customization, which is great, but the auto-detect hardware feature doesn’t work properly and can lead to major issues for less techsavvy players. The user interface is charming and well-designed, with smooth animations and intuitive navigation. The map is functional, although the layout of Hogwarts itself can be confusing at first and takes some time to get used to.
The game is also modding-friendly, which is an added bonus.

Longevity And Replayability: 6
The game offers a solid length, easily providing 30+ hours of gameplay depending on how much of the side content and trials you choose to complete. Later in the game, you unlock a build mode that allows you to design and customize your own rooms, a fun feature that I personally enjoyed for quite a few hours, though it may not appeal to everyone. This is likely the kind of game most players will experience just once, as the grind of upgrading your character from scratch may not be enticing enough to warrant a full replay. 

Fun and Overall Feeling: 7
Is it fun? Absolutely. Blasting enemies with Unforgivable Curses, exploring ancient tombs, and wielding forgotten magic—this is where Hogwarts Legacy truly shines. Puzzle-solving and collectible hunting can also be enjoyable, but the sheer volume of them eventually becomes tedious.

However, the game suffers from an identity crisis that becomes apparent around the 15-hour mark. One moment you're a student attending classes, and the next you're a ruthless killer, which seriously undermines immersion. The shift feels more comical than serious as you progress into the later stages of the game. Honestly, I felt like a raging psychopath, mowing down enemies left and right.

This would be fine if the game actually punished or even acknowledged your actions as a "dark wizard," but there are no consequences whatsoever. Don’t get me wrong, Hogwarts Legacy is still a lot of fun. But it’s hard not to feel like there was a missed opportunity here. With just a bit more depth and accountability, this game could have gone from great to truly amazing.

I’ve been playing Monster Hunter Wilds since release, and honestly, it’s been a ride. At launch, the game was gorgeous but super demanding — my old rig with an RTX 3070 could barely push 30 FPS. It makes the world feel alive and personal.

Fast forward a year, and the game has improved a ton. Performance is way better (I’d say 20–26% smoother than launch), and the gameplay has gotten harder thanks to new monsters and events. Hunts feel more intense now, and I love that challenge. The best part is how the devs are clearly listening to feedback. They’ve been refining the game nonstop, and it shows. Credit where credit’s due — Capcom nailed the updates.

Now I’m just hyped for the upcoming DLC. If it keeps up the same level of polish and improvement, this game could easily surpass World in the long run.

review:
============ [b] IMPORTANT NOTE [/b] ===============
I [b]ONLY[/b] recommend this game on discount at it's current state as of 18th June 2026

================================================

On to the review.

Monster hunter Wilds does things right and things wrong (in my opinion) regarding the latest installement in the mainline MH franchise.

I recently picked the game up and had been waiting for a nice sale due to the rumours of lack of content/monsters and then i went directly from monster hunter World: Iceborne.

I wanted to make my own opinion and didn't look anything up regarding it's content except from the initial complaints regarding PC optimization and that the content felt short when it comes to the story and the lack of monsters.

So... after clearing the mainstory and reached HR 100+ (for those who don't know HR refers to Hunter rank. Higher the rank, the more difficult missions unlocks basically) what is my take/experience?

I haven't experience any crashes and the game seems to run well on my system so no complains there.

They've added quite a lot of Quality of life features like if your inventory is full, any excessive material you gather get sent to your stash/item box, so no more dilemmas regarding what material to abondon and what to keep, making farming crafting materials easier when roaming the different places.

The gameplay has improved for some weapons, some has been changed how their unique mechanic works, some for the better some for the worse (looking at you Heavy bowgun.... where's my wyvernsnipe??).

One change i just feel that they unneccessary made more complicated than it was in MH World is simply joining a friends lobby in-game, when my friend joined me to play together he joined my lobby but he seemed to be in another instance(?) of said lobby. 
Another change i noticed was that your mount doesn't really feel responsive in a way i would expect/prefer (so this is my own opinion, i just feel that it's weird sometimes).

The campsite that you unlock just doesn't feel as earned as it was in MH World. In World you would need to find it and then gather required materials for it to be unlocked.

The different areas is a downgrade when it comes to immersive exploration, there's no true hidden parts that you need to find and move branches/roots that's in the way to unlock a new cave/path/section which is a shame.

I see what they were trying to do with the different areas  but some feels unispired but what they all have in common is that the roaming monsters looks more that the area is "bloated" you can clearly see each monster and where they are as soon as you arrive, field research is no longer a thing you seem to just by hunting learn and know everything after a few encounters.

When it comes to story and progression... the sotry is short... i mean really short and this is a comparison with Monster hunter World base game and Monster hunter world Iceborne seperately.

Felt like i barely started the game before i reached the credits and all story beats felt rushed. Without spoiling to much i would warn monster hunter world players to not even remotely expect epic hunt like the scenario where you finally face zogmagdaros that actually feels epic (untill you need to farm for materials).

Another thing that i think harms the game more than doing it any favors is that there's basically no hunts that truly feels challenging, most of the story related hunts are total pushovers so there's no monster you encounter a long the way that acts as a skillcheck where you are expected to learn and maybe also change up your gear to target it's weaknesses.
And then another thing that i think doesn't do the game any favors is how easy it is to level you hunter rank and tempered monsters basically are available way early in my opinion since the game doesn't really give you any time to learn or rather incentivises you with learning the game mechanics properly.

There's only 3 hunts that has any kind of mechanic that you actually need to learn how to do the fight. one of them isn't enjoyable (in my opinion) and SOS flares can really screw you on that one so either dedicated team or solo is my suggestion, you'll know which one i'm referring to when you encounter it.

The end-game right know is basically famring RNG materials to make powerful gear which i find is quite a dumb game design decision since you can become fatigue doing the same fight over and over.

The game is rather barebone when it comes to encounters but the gameplay feels a better although jumping from MH world there's some things that you might need to get used to, for exampel Hammer is no longer as simple that it is in World.

This is not a fullprice worthy game at all, if you want to get it, wait for a huge sale

review:
The game is peak!

Honestly, my favorite Monster Hunter game so far. The graphics are great. There is a "washed" color scheme to it but I believe that was an aesthetic choice by the developer. One I don't disagree with it. I do prefer more vibrancy in my colors so I have a mod in for that.

The weapons are all amazing. The only time they've felt better in games has been the dominance of longsword in Rise on release if you remember it. Past that, all of the weapons I've tried out has been amazing. Each feels unique and powerful. Each has a depth to them that speaks to the technical person on how to maximize damage in any given opportunity. Yet they're strong enough that if you're just a casual player just feel free to run out there and start spamming attacks, you'll do okay.

The environments themselves are great. I do prefer the smaller and faster maps of Rise but I can appreciate the work and themes of the different areas. I heard this was the same team that made World/Iceborne so I can see where all of the verticality and the winding and looping sections come from. Rise maps are a much more open and straightforward. Wilds maps are like Worlds maps. Lots of looping sections and a lot more verticality in the maps than I would generally prefer.

The story... well, story has never been Monster Hunter's strongpoint but I did get emotional. :D
But let's be real... we're here for the monsters, not the story.

There is a performance concern. I have a 9800X3D, manually tuned 64GB of RAM, 7900 XTX. I also play on widescreen and I really need to put it at 2560x1440 to actually hit solid 120+ fps and smooth gameplay. I don't framegen or scaling. I'm just want native rendering and resolution. At 3440x1440 and 3840x1600 the game is lucky to hit 100fps and generally sits around 50-80 fps across most areas and fights. There are dips down to 30fps and you can feel and see it when it happens though generally only during really expansive scenes or when loading into the hubs. Nothing at all that would preclude anyone from being able to enjoy or play the game. I do wish it was better optimized but I got no real complaints as the game runs just fine for me.

I could go on about specific things but just know that if you're an action combat gamer, or if you're at all interested in this game, please get it. It's amazing. It's a lot of fun. And don't let the mostly negative reviews turn you away. Only reason I would say to not get it is if you have a really old system and you can't afford to get a new one. But I would say that any CPU that came out within the last 8 years and any GPU from an RTX 3050/RX 6600 and up can play the game just fine. You may have to run it at 720p with sad quality settiings but the core gameplay will still be there and that's what is really good. I just hope you can one day upgrade to experience the game at high resolution and maximum quality settings. I can't project enough how awesome the monsters and environment look and how well the weapons play. :)

10.8/10 game
Get it for sure if you're at all interested and can run it!

I had The Witcher 3 sitting in my game library for years. Every time I looked at it, I told myself, "I'll play it when the time is right." Somehow, the "right time" never came. Then two of my friends (who are hardcore TW3 fans) finally got tired of my excuses and simply said, "The right time is now."

So I listened.

I honestly don't know why I waited so long, but I can say one thing with complete confidence—the wait was absolutely worth it.

From the moment I started playing, I knew this wasn't just another open-world game. It felt like stepping into a living, breathing world where every village, forest, swamp, and city had its own story to tell. Even random side quests felt better written than the main stories of many other games I have played. The story is an easy 10 out of 10. It is emotional, exciting, funny, dark, and full of moments that stay with you long after you finish playing. The choices actually matter, and sometimes the game makes you question if there was ever a "right" choice in the first place. 

What impressed me the most was how the game puts you in Geralt's shoes. You are not just controlling a character—you become him.   The world is incredibly immersive. I often started playing with one goal in mind, only to get distracted for hours just exploring caves or just riding across beautiful landscapes. 

I know I am very late to the fandom, but I have absolutely no regrets. Sometimes great games don't have an expiry date, and this is one of them. In fact, playing it years after release made me appreciate just how far ahead of its time it really was.

In a surprisingly short time, this has become one of my all-time favorite games. It gave me one of the most immersive gaming experiences I have ever had, with unforgettable characters, an incredible story, and a world that feels alive every single minute.

If you are like me and have been letting this game collect digital dust in your library, let me save you some time. Stop waiting for the "perfect moment."

The right time is now.

review:
What hasn’t already been said about The Witcher 3? Even after 10 years, I’m still tossing my two coins into the endless pit of the internet for anyone willing to invest time appreciating Roach, "accidentally" transforming Geralt into the ♥♥♥♥♥ of Rivia, and staring in absolute horror at his fully shaven face in a DLC where I then spent hours scrambling under every rock, desperately trying to glue some beard back on, because that darn ghost that possessed me and shaved everything with reckless enthusiasm.
One might say that at its core, this is a beautifully written, open-ended moral labyrinth filled with touching moments, impossible choices, and characters that make you pause and wonder if you’re actually the villain but they are all wrong. You can't sneeze in this game without someone offering you a tissue then realise, in horror, that it is a Gwent card. Every time Gwent resurfaces like an undead specter whispering “care for a round?”, I feel an overwhelming urge to hurl my Steam deck directly through the nearest window. I don’t want your cards. I don’t want your rules. I don’t want to be silently judged by shopkeepers for refusing to play fantasy Uno while the world is actively ending. I want to see this wet big dog of a man be a sassy little princess in his horrendously long list of side quests and yet… Gwent never stops following me.
Despite my lifelong vendetta against Gwent, this game remains one of the best RPGs ever made. Just know that no matter how epic your journey becomes, there’s always a man, a matron or an imaginary child nearby waiting to challenge you to a card game and your self-control to not punt them into the sun.

review:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is one of the greatest games I have ever played. Despite this sort of genre being among my least favourite (I’m not a fan of open world games), I enjoyed it very much.

The game is very story-heavy, and every dialogue feels meaningful. Every character introduced feels like they have a soul. The choices you make feel like they become part of your own history. The music is EXTREMELY good. Just imagine stumbling upon a bunch of douchebags while Shakira in the background is belly dancing and singing "LE LE LEEY LE LEEY LE LE LE LELELELELE" as everyone is trading blows. Some areas like Skellige are so beautiful that no matter how boring the activity is, you still feel like you’re doing the most fun thing ever.

My favourite part of this game is Gwent, which I highly recommend you invest deeply in. The music alone makes it the most fun card game ever.

One of the main reasons I strongly recommend this game is that, despite being released over a decade ago, it’s still being well taken care of by its developers. After 10 years, we’re getting another DLC. Thank you very much, CD PROJEKT RED!

review:
Even ten years after its release, *The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt* continues to impress with its stunning graphics that hold up exceptionally well. The game's massive open world invites exploration, offering players a landscape rich with detail and depth.

At the heart of *The Witcher 3* is a compelling storyline where choices genuinely matter. The narrative is expertly crafted, weaving together serious moments with occasional humor, creating a balanced and engaging experience that keeps players invested.

However, it’s important to approach the game with an understanding of its leveling system. I recently came across a Reddit post from a player who was frustrated with their character's slow progression. They primarily focused on the main storyline quests, which simply do not provide enough XP to keep pace with the game’s challenges. For those who prefer a more straightforward path, it's entirely possible to stick to the main quests, but be warned: you might find yourself underleveled, short on currency, and lacking essential equipment.

Ultimately, *The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt* remains a masterpiece, delivering an immersive experience that allows players to dictate their journey. Just remember, if you choose to ignore the side quests, you might miss out on some of the game’s best elements. Play your way, but be prepared for the consequences!

review:
This is the first game I played on my new PC. 
Witcher 3 is a worthy sequel and a timeless masterpiece. This game has the potential to make other open world rpgs feel dull or uninspired. Spent most of my time in Velen for subquests while got lost in Skellige due to its awesome theme. Every place feels alive and immersive as the game is made with that much care and thought.

Interacting with npcs is always fun. The dialogues feel natural and not AI generated. Even the random npc dialogues can make you crack up.

Finally Gwent, 50% of my gaming time was beating every player in the game. Its addictive and never gets repetitive.

The dlcs should be a blueprint of how devs should make expansions. It was literally like a new game with more unique characters and quests.

I will miss Geralt. Walking in his shoes as a student, then a lover and finally a father, I felt like bidding adieu to another version of me.

Chose Triss in both of my playthroughs, could not care less about the lore.

review:
9/10 - A Masterpiece With Minor Flaws

One of the greatest RPGs ever made. The Continent is breathtaking and filled with morally gray, compelling stories in every corner. Geralt's personal journey is the highlight, especially the charged and complex reunion with Yennefer. Their "vanilla romance" feels deep and authentic, full of history and fiery chemistry—it's the emotional core for many players.

Combat is visceral, the soundtrack is perfect, and the DLCs are masterpieces themselves. An unbelievable amount of top-tier content.

Why not a 10? The controls and movement can feel clunky at times, and there are some minor technical hiccups. But these are tiny complaints against a monumental achievement. A must-play.
